questions.sec: Restrictive squint — causes and Duane retraction syndrome
questions.q: All of the following are listed CONGENITAL causes of restrictive squint in the book EXCEPT:
opts: CFEOM (congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles)
questions.exp: Congenital: DRS, Brown's syndrome, CFEOM; acquired: orbital trauma, orbital tumours. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Restrictive squint — causes and Duane retraction syndrome
questions.q: The acquired causes of restrictive squint per the book are:
questions.exp: Acquired causes: orbital trauma; orbital tumours. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Restrictive squint — causes and Duane retraction syndrome
questions.q: Match the DRS type with its limitation of movement in the book's table — 1) Type I 2) Type 2 3) Type 3 … A) Abduction and adduction B) Abduction C) Adduction
questions.exp: DRS types: I — limitation of abduction; 2 — limitation of adduction; 3 — limitation of abduction and adduction. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Restrictive squint — causes and Duane retraction syndrome
questions.q: Match the DRS type with the globe retraction/palpebral fissure closure in the book's table — 1) Type I 2) Type 2 3) Type 3 … A) On abduction and adduction (d/t paradoxical innervation of both LR and MR) B) On adduction C) On abduction
questions.exp: Retraction of globe with closure of palpebral fissure: Type I — on adduction; Type 2 — on adduction; Type 3 — on abduction and adduction (d/t paradoxical innervation of both LR and MR). (Book p63)

questions.sec: Restrictive squint — causes and Duane retraction syndrome
questions.q: In Type I DRS pathology per the book, the lateral rectus is supplied by the ______ nerve instead of the 6th nerve (paradoxical).
questions.exp: Type I DRS: LR gets supplied by the 3rd nerve instead of the 6th nerve (paradoxical). (Book p63)

questions.sec: Restrictive squint — causes and Duane retraction syndrome
questions.q: In the book's Type I DRS flowchart, on the impulse for abduction via the 6th nerve the lateral rectus does not act, so there is:
questions.exp: Type I DRS: on impulse for abduction via the 6th nerve the lateral rectus does not act — no abduction. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Restrictive squint — causes and Duane retraction syndrome
questions.q: Fill up: in Type I DRS, on the impulse for adduction via the 3rd nerve both the lateral rectus and medial rectus contract, producing retraction of the globe and ______.
opts: Eversion of both the upper and lower lids
Dilation of the pupil with anisocoria
questions.exp: On impulse for adduction via the 3rd nerve: both LR and MR contract → retraction of globe → closure of palpebral fissure. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Restrictive squint — DRS diagnosis and Brown's syndrome
questions.q: The book's Type I DRS (left eye) photograph series shows: right gaze — left eye adduction present but with closure of the left palpebral fissure; primary gaze — normal, no deviation; left gaze — left eye abduction limitation. The diagnosis of DRS is made by the:
questions.exp: Diagnosis of DRS: force (forced) duction test. (Book p64)

questions.sec: Restrictive squint — DRS diagnosis and Brown's syndrome
questions.q: Brown's syndrome per the book begins with a:
questions.exp: Brown's syndrome: congenitally tight superior oblique (SO). (Book p64)

questions.sec: Restrictive squint — DRS diagnosis and Brown's syndrome
questions.q: Fill up: in Brown's syndrome the tight SO restricts its movement through the ______ (bony hook).
questions.exp: ↓ movement of SO through trochlea (bony hook) → contracture of SO. (Book p64)

questions.sec: Restrictive squint — DRS diagnosis and Brown's syndrome
questions.q: Match the Brown's syndrome step with the next event in the book's flow — 1) Contracture of the SO 2) SO fails to relax 3) Antagonist IO cannot relax … A) Restriction of elevation in adduction B) The antagonist inferior oblique is mechanically held C) The SO stays tight
questions.exp: Flow: congenitally tight SO → ↓ movement through trochlea → contracture of SO → SO fails to relax → antagonist IO cannot relax → restriction of elevation in adduction. (Book p64)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — the accommodative types
questions.q: The m/c presentation of comitant squint per the book is:
questions.exp: Comitant squint: m/c presentation — esotropia (convergent squint). (Book p64)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — the accommodative types
questions.q: Fill up: the refractive type of accommodative comitant squint in the book is esotropia associated with ______.
questions.exp: Accommodative squint: refractive — esotropia associated with hypermetropia; non-refractive — d/t high AC/A ratio. (Book p64)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — the accommodative types
questions.q: In the book's AC/A note, AC and A stand for:
questions.exp: Non-refractive accommodative squint: d/t high AC/A ratio — d/t ↑ convergence or ↓ accommodation (AC: accommodative convergence, A: accommodation); 1 D of accommodation ~ 2° convergence. (Book p64)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — the accommodative types
questions.q: Per the book, 1 D of accommodation corresponds to approximately ______ of convergence.
questions.exp: 1 D of accommodation ~ 2° convergence. (Book p64)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — the accommodative types
questions.q: The book's treatment options for non-refractive accommodative esotropia (high AC/A) include all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Bimedial recession (weakening of B/L medial recti)
questions.exp: Treatment: miotics (echothiophate); bifocal spectacles; surgery: a. bimedial recession (weakening of B/L medial recti); b. Faden surgery. (Book p64)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — non-accommodative esotropia and its treatment
questions.q: Non-accommodative esotropia in the book is AKA:
questions.exp: Non-accommodative esotropia: AKA essential infantile esotropia. (Book p65)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — non-accommodative esotropia and its treatment
questions.q: Per the book, essential infantile esotropia presents at:
questions.exp: Presentation: 4-6 months of age; no refractory error; no neurological deficit. (Book p65)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — non-accommodative esotropia and its treatment
questions.q: All of the following are listed as associated features of essential infantile esotropia in the book EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Associated with: latent horizontal nystagmus, inferior oblique overaction, dissociated vertical deviation, large angle deviation (≥15°/≥30 pd) → confusion → amblyopia of the deviated eye. (Book p65)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — non-accommodative esotropia and its treatment
questions.q: A 5-month-old with a large angle congenital squint (≥15°/≥30 pd) is at risk of amblyopia of the deviated eye, because the large angle produces:
questions.exp: Large angle deviation (≥15°/>30 pd) → confusion → amblyopia of the deviated eye. (Book p65)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — non-accommodative esotropia and its treatment
questions.q: For prevention of amblyopia, the book's occlusion therapy is:
opts: Continuous patching of the deviated eye
Intermittent alternate patching of the normal eye
questions.exp: Occlusion therapy: intermittent alternate patching of the normal eye — patch the normal eye for x days and the deviated eye for (x: age in years) days. (Book p65)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — non-accommodative esotropia and its treatment
questions.q: The book's penalization method for preventing amblyopia uses:
opts: Atropine drops in the normal eye
questions.exp: Penalization: use of atropine drops in the normal eye. (Book p65)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — non-accommodative esotropia and its treatment
questions.q: Per the book, prevention of amblyopia can be done till ______ of age, as the eyeball completes its development by 6-7 years.
questions.exp: Note: prevention of amblyopia can be done till 6 years of age (eyeball completes development by 6-7 years). (Book p65)

questions.sec: Comitant squint — non-accommodative esotropia and its treatment
questions.q: Per the book, surgery (TOC) for essential infantile esotropia is usually done at ______, and for esotropia it involves:
opts: 2 years — recession of the B/L lateral recti only
6 months — resection of I/L MR + recession of I/L LR in the same eye
1 year of age — resection of the B/L medial recti only
1 year of age — recession of I/L MR (weakening) + resection of I/L LR (strengthening)
questions.exp: Surgery (TOC): usually done at 1 year of age. In esotropia: recession of I/L MR (lengthening → weakening) + resection of I/L LR (shortening → strengthening). (Book p65)

units.title: Restrictive squint — causes and Duane retraction syndrome
units.guide: Restrictive squint causes: congenital — DRS (Duane retraction syndrome), Brown's syndrome, CFEOM (congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles); acquired — orbital trauma, orbital tumours. DRS table: Type I — limitation of abduction; retraction of globe + closure of palpebral fissure on adduction. Type 2 — limitation of adduction; retraction + closure on adduction. Type 3 — limitation of abduction and adduction; retraction + closure on abduction and adduction (d/t paradoxical innervation of both LR and MR). Type I pathology: LR gets supplied by the 3rd nerve instead of the 6th (paradoxical) — on abduction impulse via the 6th the LR does not act (no abduction); on adduction impulse via the 3rd both LR and MR contract → retraction of globe → closure of palpebral fissure.

units.title: DRS diagnosis, Brown's syndrome and comitant (accommodative) squint
units.guide: DRS photograph series (Type I, left eye): right gaze — LE adduction present with closure of the left palpebral fissure; primary gaze — normal, no deviation; left gaze — LE abduction limitation. Diagnosis: forced duction test. Brown's syndrome: congenitally tight SO → ↓ movement of SO through the trochlea (bony hook) → contracture of SO → SO fails to relax → antagonist IO cannot relax → restriction of elevation in adduction. Comitant squint: m/c presentation — esotropia (convergent squint). Types: accommodative (refractive — esotropia associated with hypermetropia; non-refractive — d/t high AC/A ratio d/t ↑ convergence or ↓ accommodation, AC: accommodative convergence, A: accommodation; 1 D accommodation ~ 2° convergence) and non-accommodative. Non-refractive treatment: miotics (echothiophate), bifocal spectacles, surgery — bimedial recession (weakening of B/L medial recti), Faden surgery.

units.title: Essential infantile esotropia — prevention of amblyopia and surgery
units.guide: Non-accommodative esotropia: AKA essential infantile esotropia; presentation 4-6 months of age; no refractory error; no neurological deficit. Associated with: latent horizontal nystagmus, inferior oblique overaction, dissociated vertical deviation, large angle deviation (≥15°/≥30 pd) → confusion → amblyopia of the deviated eye. Prevention of amblyopia: occlusion therapy — intermittent alternate patching of the normal eye (patch normal eye for x days ↔ patch deviated eye for x days, x = age in years); penalization — atropine drops in the normal eye. Prevention possible till 6 years of age (eyeball completes development by 6-7 years). Surgery (TOC): usually done at 1 year of age; for esotropia — recession of I/L MR (lengthening → weakening) + resection of I/L LR (shortening → strengthening).
